title: Thailand’s Demographic Crisis Arrives Early
gist: Thailand's fertility rate of 1.2 births per woman — comparable to economies 4-11 times richer — means deaths exceeded births by nearly 140,000 in 2025 and officials warn the population could halve in 50 years. Family-planning success, women's education and urban living costs drove the decline, while government responses (small cash handouts, fertility clinics) look underfunded amid chronic political instability.

insights.claim: Thai health officials said deaths in Thailand exceeded births by nearly 140,000 in 2025 and that, on current trends, the country's population could halve within the next 50 years.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: A shrinking population in a major ASEAN manufacturing economy points to structurally lower potential growth, a smaller tax base and fiscal strain.

themes.theme: Drivers: family planning, education, urban costs

insights.claim: Thailand's early fertility decline is attributed to greater gender equality and limited stigma against contraception; the government long encouraged contraception, abortion was broadly accessible before formal legalization in 2021, and 1990s family planning was hailed as a global success.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: The decline is culturally and institutionally entrenched, making it hard for policy to reverse.

insights.claim: Economist Sasiwimon Warunsiri Paweenawat says Thai women with a bachelor's degree or higher marry later and average about 0.5 children, and that Thai women 50 years ago averaged 6 children.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Rising female education and higher-paying jobs mechanically depress fertility, a trend set to continue.
insights.quote: Women with a bachelor’s degree or higher tend to marry later and have fewer children—on average, about 0.5 children per person.

insights.claim: More than 60 percent of Thais now live in urban areas, up from 19 percent in 1990, and Bangkok and its surroundings — home to about 25 percent of the population — have the highest cost of living, leading couples to delay children until it is 'too late'.

insights.so_what: Rapid urbanization and cost of living are core drivers, linking housing and living costs to long-run labor supply.

insights.claim: Thai childbirth support is small: a one-time 15,000 baht (~$450) grant plus up to 1,600 baht ($48) per month per child until age 6, versus a UNFPA-commissioned 2017 estimate of nearly 105,000 baht per year to raise a child — more than five times the stipend.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Incentives are an order of magnitude too small to change behavior; meaningful pronatalist spending would be a large fiscal commitment.

insights.claim: A 2024 study found even highly effective Singapore — with tax relief, childcare subsidies, housing priority and expanded leave — could only slow its birth-rate decline, not reverse it, casting doubt on lower-governance Thailand's ability to do better.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Pronatalist policies have a poor track record; investors should assume Asian fertility declines persist.

insights.claim: Thailand's health ministry plans fertility clinics in all public hospitals, intrauterine insemination clinics in every province and IVF at regional hubs, though assisted reproduction is not publicly funded and one cycle costs $1,000 to nearly $6,000 — more than median annual household income.
